criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access (private yard/premises piped connections, communal stand taps, and reliance on streams/springs) across six rural villages in Northwest Cameroon.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines community-based water management (CBWM), water management committees (WMCs), customary governance by village chiefs, and rural exclusion by urban-only state utilities (CAMWATER and CDE). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing household water access: WMC-determined upfront cash eligibility requirements for private connections, mandatory gender- and age-differentiated capital contribution rules, differentiated monthly maintenance tariffs ($2/month for private connections vs. $1/month for communal stand taps), customary enforcement sanctions by village chiefs (heavy fines and denial of funeral rite authorizations for non-contributors), and supply termination or relegation to communal standpipes due to inability to pay.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical survey data from structured questionnaires administered to 108 household heads across six villages in three rural districts (18 households per village, sampled from a list of 180 households).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household connection type (34% private connection vs. 66% communal taps, plus unimproved streams/springs), daily water consumption (35.6 l/c/d for private connections vs. 24.7 l/c/d for communal taps), collection distance (average 350 m) and time (average 71.6 min/day), affordability barriers (71 households unable to afford connection fees; 54% unable to regularly pay the $1 monthly fee), and supply termination.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (108 rural households across six villages in Mbengwi, Njinikom, and Ndu districts), exposure (CBWM/WMC tariff, upfront connection-fee eligibility, and enforcement rules), outcome (connection status, daily per-capita consumption, collection time/distance, affordability, and disconnection), and cross-sectional survey case-study design are all clearly identifiable. Note: review inclusion does not require a comparative quantitative effect size (Criterion 6 is a meta-analysis gate only).

evidence_quotes.quote: As a result, some 34% of households now have a private water connection, while 66% use communal taps. Despite this, some still relied on streams, springs and wells.

An adaptive sequential procedure was used to establish a population list of 180 households from the study area. A 60% margin error was later employed to pull a sample. This gave rise to 108 probable households (with 18 questionnaires conducted in each village).

Those with private connections pay two USDs and those using communal stand taps pay one USD per month. An upfront amount determined by the WMCs was required to be eligible for private connection. The upfront cash requirement meant that the majority of those who had private taps installed were those with permanent jobs and steady sources of income.
Results reveal that 71 households using communal taps could not afford the connection fees and 54% were unable to regularly contribute the monthly one USD connection fee.
this study shows that in some cases very poor people may be denied the right to water due to their inability to pay.

raw_response.exposure: Community-based water management (CBWM) and water management committee (WMC) governance and cost-recovery rules, including upfront cash eligibility requirements for private connections, mandatory project contributions ($1-$4 USD), monthly maintenance fees ($2 USD private vs. $1 USD communal), customary chiefdom fines/sanctions, and disconnection for non-payment.
raw_response.outcome: Household piped water access and connection type (private connection at premises vs. public stand tap vs. streams/springs), daily water consumption (litres per capita per day), water collection distance and time, affordability, and supply termination/exclusion.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural households (household heads) in six villages (Njimkang, Ngarum, Muloin, Baicham, Tugi, and Zang-Tabi) across three rural districts (Mbengwi, Njinikom, and Ndu) in Northwest Cameroon; N = 108 households sampled (18 per village) from a population list of 180 households.
raw_response.rationale: Full-text empirical study of 108 rural households across six villages in Northwest Cameroon examining how community-based water management (CBWM) institutions and rule-type cost-recovery mechanisms (WMC upfront connection-fee eligibility rules, monthly tariffs, customary sanctions by village chiefs, and disconnection for non-payment) govern household access to private piped connections versus communal standpipes, water consumption volumes, collection time/distance, and financial exclusion. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional household survey / multi-village empirical case study (structured questionnaires administered to 108 household heads across six purposefully selected villages)
